paragraphs: Among the questions that those who impugn naẓar raise: they say — "Is it not possible for you to be deluded, distracted, fall victim to a doubt, and so come to take what is false to be true? And if so, what guarantees you that you are not, across the whole range of your positions, mistaken — that you suppose you are in the right when in fact you are not?" Say to him: there is no one of us to whom what you describe might not happen. But what guarantees the man who is in the right that he is not actually mistaken is the standing of the proof that establishes the soundness of his position. Our proofs and our positions — to which we hold — are positions of many kinds, and the proof that establishes one of them is not the proof that establishes another; it is impossible for us to refute your suggestion of pervasive error by means of one single answer or one single proof. Your statement "what guarantees you that you are not mistaken in your positions?" is like the statement of someone who asks, "what is the proof that you are correct in all your positions?" — and our answer to that questioner is our answer to you: we cannot indicate the soundness of all our positions by one proof, nor demonstrate them with one demonstration. The questioner who asks for a single demonstration of the soundness of all one's positions has asked an ill-formed question, and his question is null until he asks us about each position individually so we may indicate its truth.[{2}]

We then turn the question upon him: the one who asks this question is in one of two situations. Either some things are settled in his own mind as true — whether in matters of religion or in matters of secular life — and he holds that some truth must be sought and accepted. Or he is a Sophist (sūfisṭāʾī) who claims that there is no truth at all and no knowledge at all.[{3}] If he is a Sophist, it is not obligatory to converse with him or to debate him, since he denies the manifest evident itself; the Unitarians (al-muwaḥḥidūn) have shown this in other places.[{4}] But if he is one who affirms truth and holds a position, then this question we are putting to him applies to him, whoever he is, whatever his position. And a question that is generic in this way is not binding on anyone in particular; it is unsound and unnecessary — for the implication, by his own logic, would be that everyone must abandon every position they hold, since the question applies indiscriminately to all positions. The question is therefore the very self-defeat of the questioner, since he has had to use naẓar in posing it.

They sometimes ask: "Don't you find a man holding a given view for a period of time, claiming the truth is in it, defending it and arguing for it, and then you find him later moving over to another view? His situation, while he was holding the first view, was just like his situation now, while he holds the second. What, then, guarantees you that your current positions are not subject to the same fate?" The answer is the same as in the first question. Should the questioner say, "but you yourselves would have answered exactly this way back when you held the first view," we reply: that is not, in fact, our answer; our real answer was the one we are now offering — namely, the demand that the question be put about each individual position. And the same objection that defeated the first question defeats this one: if it implies that everyone must abandon all their positions, it implies that the questioner himself must abandon his — and he has, in any case, already used naẓar in raising the question.

If someone says: "Did you know the soundness of naẓar by naẓar, or by something other than naẓar? If by naẓar — a second naẓar — then that second was known by a third, and so on; you have an infinite regress, which is unsound; and if the regress is unsound, then so is your case for naẓar." We have given the following answer: we know naẓar and qiyās by themselves. Qiyās, that is, consists in returning a thing to its analogue (radd al-shayʾ ilā naẓīrihi); its agreement with ʿilm al-iḍṭirār (necessary knowledge), its non-contradiction with the ḍarūrī knowledge on which it rests, and the impossibility for anyone to deny that two things compared in a qiyās exhibit the relation that qiyās affirms — all of these together establish the soundness of qiyās. This answer is not contested by most of the practitioners of naẓar.[{5}]

Another answer: what indicates the soundness of naẓar and istidlāl is the conviction (al-iʿtiqād al-ḥādith) that ensues upon my naẓar and my istidlāl, built upon ʿilm al-iḍṭirār. To explain: I [know by ḍarūra] that the body present to me cannot be in two places at the same time, and [I know by ḍarūra] that the elephant present to me cannot get into the eye of a needle — the needle being small and the elephant being big. I then determine, on the basis of the impossibility of the elephant's entering the eye of the needle, and on the basis of the impossibility of one body's being in two places at once, the invisible: i.e., the conviction (the inference-conclusion) that arises, which does not contradict the ʿilm al-iḍṭirār on which it is built, is the proof of the soundness of the naẓar that produced it. For if the naẓar were unsound, it would conflict with ʿilm al-iḍṭirār and would not be built upon it. This is so because, were the present instant not identical, in its essential conditions, to the instant that follows, it would not be impossible for an elephant to enter the eye of a needle — it would not be impossible either on grounds of temporal difference or on grounds of my presence at the event. Rather, it is impossible because such an event would entail that the elephant be at once small (smaller than the needle's eye, when it enters) and big (bigger than the needle's eye, since it is an elephant); and it is contradictory that a thing be small (and) not small, big (and) not big. And since the impossibility of this in the invisible is identical to the impossibility in the visible — because the cause is the same, and there is no way to differentiate the two — it follows that the invisible must be inferred from the visible (ḥaml al-ghāʾib ʿalā al-shāhid), and that the knowledge to which this naẓar leads is itself the proof of the soundness of the naẓar; for were it not sound, it would not lead to knowledge. The supposition of our opponents — that qiyās yields qiyās in an infinite regress and never to knowledge — is thereby null and void. For we have shown that what indicates the soundness of naẓar is precisely the correct inference's terminating in a conviction built upon, and consistent with, ʿilm al-iḍṭirār. The same response binds the questioner of the original objection: he, in posing the question, has already used naẓar and qiyās, since he has treated the ruling on the "second naẓar" as identical to the ruling on the "first naẓar" — and that is itself an inferential move. And if his qiyās is unsound, so is his question.

Another set of respondents have answered that we know "the ruling of a thing is the ruling of its like" by iḍṭirār — i.e., that the very principle of analogical inference is itself a piece of ʿilm ḍarūrī. They thereby claim that the soundness of qiyās is necessary, immediate knowledge.[{7}]

If someone asks: imagine a man newly arrived from a far country — China, say, or somewhere of the kind — and a crowd of people of different religious schools meets him: among them a Dahrī, a Manichaean, a Magian, a Sabian, a Jew, a Christian, and a Muslim. Each one of them calls him to his school and argues for the truth of his school. What is the man obligated to do? Whom should he answer first? Say: if the man is rational and of full age, and the Dahrī and the Manichaean and the rest of the religious parties call him to their views, and the Monotheist calls him to his, then what is obligatory on him before he begins to investigate is to consider all of the proposed views and weigh which of these schools is the safest in its outcome, were he to err — which has the most security and the least to fear when there is a dispute about it. He should adopt that one provisionally and then begin the investigation. If he does this, and pursues baḥth in a way that is not contaminated by personal inclination (mayl) or by mere taqlīd, it will not be long before the truth becomes evident to him. And if he asks, "but which view has the most safety and the least to fear?", we will address that later.[{8}] Now: if the questioner who raises the objection himself holds some view or affiliates with some school, then the same response applies to him; and if he is merely attempting to undermine baḥth and naẓar as such, then his question turns back against him — for the new arrival cannot, on the questioner's own logic, abandon investigation, since he has seen people calling him to their respective views, and the questioner does not, on his own account, hold that the abandonment of investigation is itself obligatory.[{9}]

In every case: whoever claims to abolish the probative force of reason (ḥujjat al-ʿaql) — by what ḥujja will he abolish it? If he claims to do so by a khabar, he will be asked what is the proof of that khabar's soundness; he will then, at that point, be forced to take refuge in the testimony of his own intellect, which will leave him in the position of a man who cries out with his voice: "O mankind, know that I am mute and incapable of speech!" — the very act by which he attempts to establish his thesis falsifies it.[{10}] If he claims to abolish naẓar by ḍarūra or by ḥiss (necessity or sense), the unsoundness of that has already been shown in Babs 2 and 3. And if he takes refuge in al-ʿaql itself, the impossibility of his position is manifest, since he is using the very thing he claims to abolish.

And what further proves the soundness of the indication of reason (dilālat al-ʿaql) and the binding force of its argument (ḥujja) is this: we find the soul instinctively inclined, when confronted with anything it does not recognize, to return to the rational faculty in order to discriminate it truly. And what further proves the binding force of reason and the soundness of its indication is this: we find that the commandment of God is binding…[{11}] All mankind — believers and unbelievers alike — censure the disregarder when he is rebuked by appeal to his own intellect; were the intellect not active in cognition[{12}] […].

We have now established the obligation of baḥth, naẓar, and qiyās, and the corruption of taqlīd, with what suffices, and have answered the principal objections of those who would refute it. All that we have said about this is binding both in uṣūl (theological foundations) and in furūʿ (legal branches) alike — by furūʿ I mean the farāʾiḍ and the waṣāyā (the commandments and the prohibitions).[{13}] We now present what is in Scripture of the statements that obligate inquiry and the use of al-maʿqūl — passing on, by that, to the next bab.[{14}] ---
